assessmentSummary.identity: A planned linear approach, approximately 45-degree sidestep cut, and immediate acceleration through a marked exit lane. The baseline is preplanned and alternates both cut directions; reactive cueing is a controlled variant rather than part of the base identity.
currentCardFindings: The title and purpose match the NSCA run-and-cut sequence, but the current card omits approach distance, cut-foot convention, exit distance, valid angle tolerance, surface, lane, and timing boundaries.
The existing one-to-ten legacy load value understates rapid body-mass braking and repropulsion despite no external implement.
Four sets of two may be reasonable for high-quality work, but the legacy RPE 9 and 12-second work field can encourage conditioning unless each repetition is individually reset.
All five media links are candidate-only. The closest candidate names linear acceleration to a coach-led 45-degree cut, but full exact-version review remains outstanding.

coachCues: See the lane before the plant
Turn hips trunk and eyes together
athleteInstructions: Accelerate from the start marker at the assigned speed
Control speed across the final approach steps
Plant the foot opposite the new direction
Accelerate immediately through the finish marker

calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: The proposed difficulty and dose are conservative library judgments, not validated universal thresholds. Exact angle, approach velocity, and technique materially change load.

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as the planned 45-degree cut with immediate exit acceleration. Keep reactive cueing, crossover technique, and entry-speed progressions as reviewed variants; do not merge the terminal-stick or diagonal-bound identities.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Use a declared straight approach lane, a marked approximately 45-degree exit lane, and a protected run-out. Accelerate at the assigned intent, distribute braking across the final approach steps, use the declared sidestep-cut plant relationship, redirect into the exit lane, and accelerate immediately without a false step. One repetition ends after the declared exit distance and controlled deceleration. This is not a terminal-stick drill, a 90-degree cut, a diagonal bound, a reactive-cue drill, or a ball-control task.

environment.space: one athlete per approach-cut-exit lane; release only after the prior athlete clears the run-out
inspection: approach, cut marker, exit lane, run-out, surface, footwear, and weather fit the declared speed
coach can view braking, plant, trunk, knee, foot, exit, and finish
communication, release order, and stop route are clear

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Youth training requires qualified supervision, technically appropriate progression, safe environments, and attention to individual readiness.
Stop 45-Degree Cut and Reaccelerate for pain, guarding, slipping, repeated loss of alignment or balance, unsafe lane traffic, or a material decline in the assigned movement quality.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Youth development should be individualized, progressive, and based on current physical and psychosocial readiness rather than a fixed exercise-card level.

Make 45-Degree Cut and Reaccelerate accessible with a walk-through, shorter approach or projection, lower speed, visible floor arrows, longer reset, and a simpler prerequisite task; do not label the exercise itself beginner or advanced.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.
The supplied links are candidate demonstrations only. oEmbed availability was checked, but exact sequence, safety, cue quality, captions, full content, reviewer identity, and approval remain pending.
The NSCA run-and-cut exercise uses a five-yard approach, deceleration into a cut step, and immediate acceleration approximately 45 degrees away.
45-Degree Cut and Reaccelerate matches that planned approach-cut-exit identity when approach, plant, angle, and immediate acceleration are explicit.

evidence.sourceTitle: Center of mass direction and speed during a 45-degree change of direction task performed with maximal effort
evidence.sourcePublisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
claims: A maximal 45-degree task shares direction change across approach, execution, and following steps.
Classify the full approach-to-exit sequence, plant side, sidestep technique, approximate angle, and planned cue state rather than only the named plant.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effect of foot strike patterns and angles on the biomechanics of side-step cutting
claims: Forty-five-degree sidestep cutting produces ankle, knee, hip, ground-reaction-force, and lower-limb muscle demands during loading and propulsion.
Represent ankle and subtalar stabilization, knee and hip force acceptance, pelvis and trunk control, and the lower-limb musculature that brakes and reaccelerates the body.

evidence.sourceTitle: Center of mass direction and speed during a 45-degree change of direction task performed with maximal effort
evidence.sourcePublisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
claims: At maximal effort, the execution step contributed only part of the 45-degree direction change while approach and following steps also redirected center-of-mass velocity.
The card must coach distributed braking and a coordinated following step rather than a single isolated plant claimed to create the entire angle.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Determinants of Performance and Injury Risk During Cutting: A Performance-Injury Conflict?
claims: Cut performance and injury-related loading depend on interacting whole-body mechanics, angle, speed, and task strategy.

Score technical complexity and physical body-mass demand directly, derive overall as their maximum, and retain supervision, consequence, impact, coordination, and work capacity as separate planning dimensions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration: A Review with Implications for Random Intermittent Multi-Directional Sports
claims: Horizontal deceleration exposes athletes to high eccentric forces, and braking demands rise with momentum and task constraints.
Log approach speed, side, contact count, exit distance, surface, total cutting and sprint exposure, and technique degradation; bodyweight does not mean low load.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of the Cutting Alignment Scoring Tool (CAST) to Assess Trunk and Limb Alignment During a 45-Degree Side-Step Cut
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
claims: Reliable qualitative observation of 45-degree side-step cutting depends on standardized task geometry and visible alignment.
45-Degree Cut and Reaccelerate requires a clear approach, cut marker, exit lane and runoff, reliable traction, no cross traffic, and views that show trunk, hip, knee, and foot behavior.
The professional exercise alternates cuts to the right and left and emphasizes immediate post-cut acceleration.
Low repetition counts and full recovery are programming inferences intended to preserve speed and mechanics; the cited source does not establish a universal set-rest prescription.
The NSCA coaching points keep the plant foot forward, body weight inside the base of support, and acceleration immediate after the cut.
Instructions must also identify approach speed, plant side, exit lane and distance, valid angle tolerance, reset, and what invalidates a repetition.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Determinants of Performance and Injury Risk During Cutting: A Performance-Injury Conflict?
claims: Planned cutting mechanics are an appropriate motor-learning foundation before adding unanticipated perceptual demands.
Place 45-Degree Cut and Reaccelerate before fatigue when output is the goal, or use a slower technical profile; do not turn high-intent cutting into conditioning.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of the Cutting Alignment Scoring Tool (CAST) to Assess Trunk and Limb Alignment During a 45-Degree Side-Step Cut
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
claims: Observable trunk and limb alignment features can support structured feedback during a 45-degree sidestep cut.
Athlete support should show the lane, braking steps, correct plant, whole-body orientation, immediate first exit step, invalid false step, and clear pain or confidence stop guidance.

evidence.sourceTitle: Center of mass direction and speed during a 45-degree change of direction task performed with maximal effort
evidence.sourcePublisher: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
claims: Approach, execution, and following steps each contribute to the completed 45-degree task.
Coach support should standardize approach and exit distances, observe multiple steps, compare both sides, distinguish sidestep from crossover strategy, and progress one variable at a time.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Determinants of Performance and Injury Risk During Cutting: A Performance-Injury Conflict?
claims: Cutting task demands and mechanics change with angle, anticipated versus unanticipated conditions, and technique.
Terminal hold, angle, cue predictability, cut technique, entry speed, and ball or opponent task are controlled identity or variant decisions and must not be silently conflated.

alternateAssessments.name: 45-Degree Cut-and-Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: A deliberate held terminal position removes immediate acceleration and changes the primary outcome from exit speed to braking control.

alternateAssessments.name: Reactive 45-Degree Cut
alternateAssessments.rationale: An unpredictable directional cue adds perception and response selection while preserving the same physical cut-and-exit sequence.

alternateAssessments.name: Crossover 45-Degree Cut and Reaccelerate
alternateAssessments.rationale: Crossover cutting changes the plant relationship and force strategy but can remain a technique variant under a matched route and outcome.

alternateAssessments.name: 90-Degree Speed Cut
alternateAssessments.rationale: The sharper angle changes braking, translation, joint loading, lane geometry, and performance strategy.

alternateAssessments.name: Ball-Carry 45-Degree Cut and Reaccelerate
alternateAssessments.rationale: Adding a ball or implement imposes a motor-motor task and may alter trunk strategy while the locomotor identity remains the same.
